native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Increasing education expenditure shows no positive association with per-capita GDP growth in either developing countries (LMC proxy) or Sub-Saharan Africa, and the association is weakest in SSA: in LMC a 1-pp higher (or rising) education-expenditure share of GNI is associated with 2–4 pp lower subsequent annual income growth (ADL with controls β=−2.99, p<0.001; change-based β=−2.49, p=0.036), while SSA — which spent a persistently higher share of GNI on education (4.30% vs 3.50%) and expanded enrollment rapidly — grew per-capita income far more slowly (+5.1% vs +13.8% over 2011–2015), implying lower marginal income returns to education expenditure in SSA. Direct SSA coefficients are unreliable (income series only 2011–2015) and all estimates are associative, not causal.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded worldbank_education_gdp.csv (12 rows = 2 group aggregates × 6 WDI series × 41 years 1975–2015; missing cells empty, no '..' placeholders). Reshaped to long panel; ADF/DW diagnostics (non-stationary levels → first-differenced and ADL specifications with Newey-West HAC errors); LMC regressions of Δlog GNI pc on lagged education-expenditure share (level and change versions, with/without enrollment, exports-growth and LFPR controls); common-window 2011–2015 comparison with pooled group×education interaction and block-bootstrap inference (B=5000); outlier robustness check (SSA −43.3% exports growth retained, winsorization inconsequential); long-horizon trajectory comparison of expenditure shares and enrollment gains. Scripts: analysis/01_inspect.py, analysis/02_analysis.py; outputs: analysis/results.json.

sub_hypo.text: Education expenditure shows no positive association with per-capita income growth in either group, with the weakest association and implied lower marginal income returns in SSA.
sub_hypo.context: SSA versus LMC, using long-horizon trajectories and a common-window 2011–2015 comparison with pooled group-by-education interaction and block-bootstrap inference. Direct SSA coefficients are unreliable because its income series covers only 2011–2015; all estimates are associative, not causal.

SSA's higher spending coupled with slower income growth implies lower marginal income returns to education expenditure, subject to unreliable direct SSA coefficients and no causal interpretation.
